replication_title: “Eavesdropping on Happiness” Revisited: A Pooled, Multisample Replication of the Association Between Life Satisfaction and Observed Daily Conversation Quantity and Quality
explanation: The authors explicitly state that the small talk effect 'did not replicate,' concluding that 'The negative correlation suggested by the underpowered original study seems to have been a false-positive finding.' The pooled Bayesian estimate was r = .05 (95% CI [-.04, .14]), with the credible interval containing zero.

description: Happier individuals engage in more substantive conversations in daily life, as measured by the Electronically Activated Recorder (EAR)
original_authors: Mehl MR; Vazire S.; Holleran SE; Clark CS
original_title: Eavesdropping on happiness: Well-being is related to having less small talk and more substantive conversations
replication_authors: Anne Milek; Emily A. Butler; Allison M. Tackman; Deanna M. Kaplan; Charles L. Raison; David A. Sbarra; Simine Vazire; Matthias R. Mehl
replication_title: “Eavesdropping on Happiness” Revisited: A Pooled, Multisample Replication of the Association Between Life Satisfaction and Observed Daily Conversation Quantity and Quality
explanation: The authors state: 'In accordance with the original findings reported by Mehl and colleagues (2010), we found solid evidence that engaging in substantive conversations was moderately associated with life satisfaction.' The pooled Bayesian estimate was r = .23 (95% CI [.14, .32]), similar in direction and magnitude to the original.

description: Science interest interacts with family SES and national GDP in predicting science achievement, such that students from more economically advantaged families and nations show a stronger positive association between science interest and science knowledge
original_authors: Elliot M. Tucker-Drob; Amanda K. Cheung; Daniel A. Briley
original_title: Gross domestic product, science interest, and science achievement: A Person × Nation interaction
replication_authors: Anqing Zheng; Elliot M. Tucker-Drob; Daniel A. Briley
replication_title: National Gross Domestic Product, Science Interest, and Science Achievement: A Direct Replication and Extension of the Tucker-Drob, Cheung, and Briley (2014) Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusion: 'In this direct replication and extension of the study by [Tucker-Drob et al.], we found similar results. There was a stronger association between science interest and science knowledge in students from economically advantaged homes and nations.' The main effects and key interaction effects replicated in the same direction and with similar statistical significance, though interaction magnitudes decreased over the decade (suggesting true moderation over time rather than replication failure).

replication_title: Correlates of Hallucinatory Experiences in the General Population: An International Multisite Replication Study
explanation: The replication found no correlation between imagine-to-hear source errors and CAPS score (r_S = .02, p = .461), and equivalence testing confirmed the effect was indistinguishable from zero. The authors explicitly state 'This fails to conceptually replicate previous studies' regarding source monitoring.

replication_title: Correlates of Hallucinatory Experiences in the General Population: An International Multisite Replication Study
explanation: No correlation was found between CAPS score and dichotic listening performance in either the nonforced condition (r_S = .006, p = .842) or the forced-left condition (r_S = .022, p = .435), with equivalence testing confirming effects indistinguishable from zero. Authors explicitly note this 'fails to conceptually replicate previous studies'.

replication_title: Correlates of Hallucinatory Experiences in the General Population: An International Multisite Replication Study
explanation: No association was found between mean digit span and CAPS score (r_S = -.02, p = .552), with equivalence testing indicating the effect was indistinguishable from zero. This conceptually fails to replicate the hypothesized link between verbal working memory and hallucinatory experiences.

description: False-alarm rate on an auditory signal detection task is positively associated with hallucinatory experiences in the general population

replication_title: Correlates of Hallucinatory Experiences in the General Population: An International Multisite Replication Study
explanation: A significant positive association was found between CAPS score and false-alarm rate (r_S = .14, 95% CI [.06, .22], p < .001), consistent with the original finding. The authors discuss this as confirming that 'hallucinatory experiences were associated with false perceptions and a lower response criterion on an auditory signal detection paradigm'.

replication_title: Correlates of Hallucinatory Experiences in the General Population: An International Multisite Replication Study
explanation: A significant positive correlation was found between CAPS total and ACE score (r_S = .24, 95% CI [.19, .29], p < .001), confirming the hypothesized link. The authors state the findings were 'consistent with previous evidence both in psychosis patients and in the general population'.

description: Individual items of the AQ-10 autism screening instrument show differential item functioning (DIF) by sex, but there is no differential test functioning (DTF) overall — meaning the AQ-10 total score is not biased against females

replication_title: Investigating Sex Bias in the AQ-10: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly state their study is 'a replication of a recent study by [16]' and conclude: 'our results broadly replicated this result: we found no evidence for statistically significant bias at the test score level overall, or at the trait level corresponding to a test score of 6 in females.' The same DIF/DTF methodology was used with the same anchor items in an independent clinical and community sample.

description: Ultra-brief defusion (but not acceptance) interventions reduce chocolate consumption as measured by a bag-carry method, compared to an active control condition
original_authors: Kim T. Jenkins; Katy Tapper
original_title: Resisting chocolate temptation using a brief mindfulness strategy
replication_authors: Lee Hulbert-Williams; Nick J. Hulbert-Williams; Wendy Nicholls; Sian Williamson; Jivone Poonia; Kevin D. Hochard
replication_title: Ultra-brief non-expert-delivered defusion and acceptance exercises for food cravings: A partial replication study
explanation: The paper explicitly calls itself a 'partial replication' of Jenkins and Tapper (2014), following the same bag method paradigm with improved intervention scripts. The defusion finding was replicated; notably, the improved acceptance intervention also worked, which the authors attribute to enhancements in intervention design rather than failure of the original: 'The effects observed for our defusion technique parallel, and are greater still than those of [20], whilst our acceptance technique was successful in reducing cravings, whilst that of Jenkins and Tapper was not.'

description: A defusion intervention reduces post-restriction behavioural rebound consumption of chocolate, without reducing self-reported cravings
original_authors: Nic Hooper; Emily K. Sandoz; Jennifer Ashton; Amelia Clarke; Louise McHugh
original_title: Comparing thought suppression and acceptance as coping techniques for food cravings
replication_authors: Lee Hulbert-Williams; Nick J. Hulbert-Williams; Wendy Nicholls; Sian Williamson; Jivone Poonia; Kevin D. Hochard
replication_title: Ultra-brief non-expert-delivered defusion and acceptance exercises for food cravings: A partial replication study
explanation: The paper explicitly follows the method of Hooper et al. (2012) by incorporating a behavioral rebound measure, and replicates the key finding that defusion reduces rebound consumption. The current study found a significant effect of intervention on post-experiment rebound (F(2,60)=6.08, p=.004, η²par=.17), and similarly found no significant reduction in self-reported cravings, consistent with Hooper et al.'s original findings (η²=.27 for rebound, η²=.02 for cravings).

description: 26% of children diagnosed with ADHD have epileptiform discharges (ED) detectable by EEG, suggesting EEG should be considered prior to prescribing stimulant medications

replication_title: The Utility of EEG in Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a replication study and conclude they concur with the 2011 findings: 'Our study concluded that one-third of our pediatric ADHD population have epileptiform activity compared with the one-fourth found in the study conducted in 2011... Overall, this replication study provides further evidence for the routine use of EEG.' When excluding comorbid cases, the replication found exactly 26% ED prevalence, matching the original finding.

description: Reasons for attending systemic sclerosis support groups can be grouped into three main factors: (1) interpersonal and social support, (2) disease treatment and symptom management strategies, and (3) other aspects of living with systemic sclerosis, as identified in a European and Australian sample
original_authors: Stephanie T. Gumuchian; Vanessa C. Delisle; Linda Kwakkenbos; Mia Pépin; Marie-Eve Carrier; Vanessa L. Malcarne; Sandra Peláez; Ghassan El-Baalbaki; Brett D. Thombs

replication_title: Reasons for attending support groups and organizational preferences: A replication study using the North American Scleroderma Support Group Survey
replication_journal: Journal of Scleroderma and Related Disorders
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusions: 'The three main reasons to attend support groups that were identified in a previous study [16] replicated well in the current study.' The same three-factor structure was confirmed via CFA (TLI = 0.97, CFI = 0.97, RMSEA = 0.06) in a North American sample, and organizational preferences were also found to be similar.

description: Polymorphisms in intron 4 of the estrogen receptor alpha gene (ESR1), specifically haplotypes of rs3020314 and rs1884051, are associated with reduced risk of hip fractures in a Chinese population
original_authors: Jin-Tang Wang; Yan Guo; Tie-Lin Yang; Xiang-Hong Xu; Shan-Shan Dong; Meng Li; Tian-Qing Li; Yuan Chen; Hong-Wen Deng

replication_title: Haplotypes of intron 4 of the estrogen receptor alpha gene and hip fractures: a replication study in Caucasians
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'Our study, aimed to replicate those findings in Caucasians, confirmed a strong association of the haplotypes of the intron 4 of ESR1 with hip fractures, particularly in women.' The Conclusion reaffirms: 'we have confirmed a significant association of genetic variants in the region of exon 4-intron 4 of the ESR1 and hip fractures in the Caucasian women.' The haplotypic analysis showed significant association (omnibus test p = 0.006 in whole group, p = 0.00005 in women).

description: The G-allele of SNP rs2891168 on chromosome 9p21 is associated with increased susceptibility to coronary artery disease (CAD)/myocardial infarction (MI) but not with type 2 diabetes
original_authors: Helen M. Broadbent; John F. Peden; Stefan Lorkowski; Anuj Goel; Halit Ongen; Fiona Green; Robert Clarke; Rory Collins; Maria Grazia Franzosi; Gianni Tognoni; Udo Seedorf; Stephan Rust; Per Eriksson; Anders Hamsten; Martin Farrall; Hugh Watkins

replication_title: Common genetic variants on chromosome 9p21 are associated with myocardial infarction and type 2 diabetes in an Italian population
explanation: The authors explicitly call their work a 'replication study' and confirm the association: 'The main finding of the present study is therefore its ability to replicate the analysis done in the European PROCARDIS population on an independent cohort of Italians.' SNP rs2891168 was significantly associated with MI (p = 0.03, OR = 1.20, 95% CI 1.02–1.41) but not T2D, matching the original direction.

original_authors: Helen M. Broadbent; John F. Peden; Stefan Lorkowski; Anuj Goel; Halit Ongen; Fiona Green; Robert Clarke; Rory Collins; Maria Grazia Franzosi; Gianni Tognoni; Udo Seedorf; Stephan Rust; Per Eriksson; Anders Hamsten; Martin Farrall; Hugh Watkins

replication_title: Common genetic variants on chromosome 9p21 are associated with myocardial infarction and type 2 diabetes in an Italian population
explanation: The Italian replication study found that rs10811661 T-allele was significantly associated with T2D (OR = 1.27, 95% CI 1.04–1.55, p = 0.02) but not MI, confirming the PROCARDIS hypothesis of independent susceptibility variants. The authors note 'it is important to note that rs10811661 is a genetic risk factor for T2D in the Italian population,' and pooled results further confirmed the association across European populations.

Using a different study design (extremely discordant sibpairs vs. case-control GWAS) and a neovascular-only AMD cohort, they confirmed 23 of 35 dbGAP SNPs, including key variants on chromosomes 1q (CFH, CFHR4, CFHR2, CFHR5, F13B, ASPM, ZBTB41), 2q (MAP2), and 10q26 (PLEKHA1/HTRA1). The 12 non-replicated SNPs (on 3p, 4q, 10q24, 11q, 12q) have a plausible biological explanation — the authors suggest they may predispose to the geographic atrophy subtype rather than neovascular AMD. Result classified as 'success' because the core findings on chromosomes 1, 2, and 10 were clearly confirmed. Confidence upgraded to high: despite the original being a database resource rather than a traditional publication, the replication relationship is unambiguous from the authors' own framing. Subdiscipline corrected from 'pharmacology and toxicology' to 'ophthalmology'.

explanation: The authors explicitly state this is 'the first replication study for B4DT on panic disorder' conducted at a new clinic with different therapists, and conclude: 'The results indicate that the B4DT can be replicated at other clinics using other therapists and still obtained the same promising results.' They found similar outcomes (no significant difference at post-treatment, p = .352) and high remission rates (80.0% at post-treatment, 86.7% at follow-up).

The genotype (p=0.92) and allele frequency (p=0.72) showed no significant differences between patients and controls.

explanation: The replication found that 'rs1800469 was found to be associated with the curve severity,' with genotype TT showing significantly higher Cobb angles (39.1° ± 12.8°) than CT (34.8° ± 11.1°) or CC (32.1° ± 10.6°), p<0.01, consistent with the original study's finding.

explanation: The authors state that the association between rs1800469 and age of onset, as reported by Ryzhkov et al., 'was not replicated in our analysis' (p=0.78), showing no significant difference in age of onset across genotypes CC, CT, and TT.

explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'the previously reported association of AKAP2 with the susceptibility of AIS in Chinese population was not replicated in the present study.' No cases of the c.2645A > C mutation were found in 1254 AIS patients and 1232 controls, no common SNPs covering AKAP2 were significantly associated with AIS, and AKAP2 mRNA expression was comparable between cases and controls (p = 0.66).

explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'HSPG2 gene was not associated with the susceptibility or the phenotypes of AIS in the Chinese population.' No mutations of p.Asn786Ser were found in any of the 3,336 subjects (1,752 patients and 1,584 controls), and HSPG2 mRNA expression was comparable between patients and controls (p = 0.29), directly failing to replicate the original association finding in a different population.

explanation: The replication successfully replicated only one of nine factors: 'return-to-work expectancy was replicated as a statistically significant modifiable prognostic factor of high societal costs.' Six other factors (pain severity, self-perceived health, sleep quality, work satisfaction, disability, long-lasting disorder expectation) showed inconsistent results across the two studies, while depressive symptoms and health literacy showed no prognostic value in both samples.

explanation: The authors explicitly describe this as a 'replication study' comparing UNC vignettes (2015-2016) to the original UMN study. They find mixed results: the institutions were significantly different in the proportion of cases depicting race (difference 0.20; 95% CI 0.15-0.25), yet the Discussion concludes that 'reporting race and ethnicity is not distinctly different for a study conducted 20 years ago,' with the common pattern of male over-representation and largely unspecified race persisting at both schools.

explanation: The replication confirmed the existence of six dementia care dyad subgroups and replicated several key directional patterns (e.g., worse QoL for adult-child vs. couple relationships, worse caregiver health in couple classes with older female caregivers). However, the authors note 'considerable differences are also evident' in class sizes, class-forming indicators, two original classes could not be replicated, and one new class appeared, resulting in qualified rather than full support.

The Discussion confirms that 'the improved scoring of DEMQOL and DEMQOL-Proxy previously developed in a heterogeneous sample... also holds for the specific subset of people with a diagnosis of dementia,' and the Conclusion states the results are 'similar enough to our previous findings to indicate that the improved scoring is appropriate for the specific sub-sample with a diagnosis of dementia.'

explanation: Reviewer verified: genuinely ambiguous. The Tao et al. 7-CpG signature (represented by 16 CpGs available in MCCS) showed a clear unadjusted association with breast cancer-specific survival (Model 0: HR=1.41, 95%CI 1.13-1.75, P=0.002; Model 1: HR=1.40, P=0.003), but this attenuated substantially after adjustment for clinical variables (Model 2: HR=1.22, 95%CI 0.98-1.53, P=0.08; Model 3: HR=1.22, 95%CI 0.96-1.55, P=0.10). The abstract counts '2 out of 3' multi-CpG signatures as replicated (Du=failure, Liu=success), implying the authors consider Tao replicated, likely based on the unadjusted signal. However, the fully adjusted Model 3 CI crosses 1 and P=0.10, suggesting the unadjusted association may be confounded by stage/subtype. Classification kept as 'inconclusive' because there is a real signal in unadjusted models but it does not survive full adjustment — reasonable people could classify this as either partial success or failure.

replication_title: Results of the preclinical multicenter randomized controlled paclitaxel-induced neuropathy prevention replication study (PINPRICS)
explanation: Reviewer reclassified from 'failure' to 'inconclusive'. The nilotinib arm was never tested in the PINPRICS prevention study because supralinear toxicity was discovered during the dose-confirmation phase (PINPRICS-DC) when nilotinib was co-administered intraperitoneally with paclitaxel — all nilotinib-treated animals had to be prematurely sacrificed, even at greatly reduced doses (0.4-10 mg/kg). The original study (Leblanc et al. 2018) used oral nilotinib at 100 mg/kg; the switch to intraperitoneal administration (required for blinding across all arms) introduced the fatal toxicity. Because the neuroprotective hypothesis was never actually tested, 'failure' is not the correct classification — the replication attempt was aborted due to a safety issue, making the outcome genuinely inconclusive. The authors explicitly note this route-of-administration difference as a key limitation.

replication_title: Results of the preclinical multicenter randomized controlled paclitaxel-induced neuropathy prevention replication study (PINPRICS)
explanation: Lithium carbonate showed a numerical trend toward neuroprotection but did not reach statistical significance on either endpoint. On the primary endpoint (SNAP amplitude at day 14), Li/PTX was 100% ± 26% of baseline vs VEH/PTX at 83% ± 12%. On the secondary endpoint (von Frey mechanical withdrawal threshold), Li/PTX was 55% ± 30% vs VEH/PTX at 43% ± 16%. Neither difference was statistically significant. The study was severely underpowered: planned n=15 per group but 49 of 198 animals were prematurely sacrificed due to unexpectedly rapid tumor growth, leaving only day 14 data (n=10 per group) instead of the prespecified day 42 primary endpoint. The authors state the results 'although showing a trend toward neuroprotection for lithium carbonate...yielded no significant results.' Confidence remains medium because the ambiguity is genuine — the underpowered design means neither confirmation nor refutation of the original finding can be claimed.

The authors explicitly note this inconsistency: 'such risk allele for autoimmune disease seemed to be protective against allergy in Han Chinese.' Most other SNPs from Hinds et al. did not replicate. Confidence remains medium because the mixed directionality makes any single summary classification inherently debatable.

The authors attribute this to population heterogeneity (different LD patterns: risk allele frequency 0.09 in Chinese vs 0.16 in Europeans). original_title: Derivation of a prediction model for a diagnosis of depression in young adults: a matched case-control study using electronic primary care records
replication_authors: David Nickson; Henrik Singmann; Caroline Meyer; Carla Toro; Lukasz Walasek

explanation: The authors explicitly conclude that 'our results demonstrate that the work of Nichols et al. is largely reproducible and replicable,' finding that new models trained on a newer dataset achieved AUC-ROCs of approximately 0.88, and out-of-sample predictions using the original NRCBM coefficients also performed well (average AUC 0.855), confirming the robustness of the original findings.

original_authors: David A. M. Peterson; Lori A. Biederman; David Andersen; Tessa M. Ditonto; Kevin Roe

replication_authors: Lisa D. Mitchem; Rachel L. Rupnow; Collin P. Jaeger; Marissa N. Pezdek; Brenda K. Anak Ganeng; Karen E. Samonds; Heather E. Bergan-Roller
replication_title: Replication of an Intervention to Mitigate Gender Bias in Student Evaluations of Teaching Yields Variable Results Across a Biology Department
explanation: The authors explicitly call this a 'conceptual replication' and conclude: 'our findings do not support the consistent replicability of the original work scaled to the department level.' The AntiBias statement produced a significant interaction effect in only 1 of 3 semesters (Fall 2021), with no effect in Spring 2021 or Spring 2022, leading the authors to state 'Unlike [55], our findings at the departmental level do not support that the simple inclusion of an Antibias statement mitigates the complex issue of gender biases toward instructors in SETs.'

explanation: The paper explicitly states in its Discussion: 'The results of previous studies on the I.Q. of patients with Turner's Syndrome are confirmed by the findings of the present study.' The replication (N=12) found significantly higher Verbal IQ than Performance IQ and a significant Verbal Comprehension vs Perceptual Organization discrepancy, consistent with Shaffer (1962).

description: Single-night total sleep deprivation therapy improves mood in psychotic depressive patients, with all psychotic depressives showing improvement while neurotic depressives and normal subjects were unaffected or felt worse
original_authors: Pflug, B.; Tolle, R.
original_title: Die behandlung endogener depressionen durch schlafentzug
original_journal: Zentralblatt für die Gesamte Neurologie und Psychiatrie
replication_authors: Bhanji S.; Roy GA
replication_title: The Treatment of Psychotic Depression by Sleep Deprivation: A Replication Study
explanation: Reviewer verification: The paper explicitly titles itself 'A Replication Study' of Pflug & Tolle's sleep deprivation therapy. Of 28 patients completing treatment, 17 (61%) showed improvement (12 Good, 5 Excellent) while 11 (39%) were rated Poor. This is directionally consistent with Pflug & Tolle's original finding that all psychotic depressives improved, but substantially attenuated (61% vs 100%). The authors acknowledge their results are 'less impressive than elsewhere' and conclude with hedged language: sleep deprivation 'may be of value' and 'further study appears warranted.' Confidence remains medium because: (1) the effect is much weaker than the original, (2) the study was open and uncontrolled, (3) 32/39 patients were on concurrent antidepressant medication (vs drug-free in the original), (4) placebo effects and spontaneous remission cannot be ruled out, and (5) no statistical tests were performed on the core hypothesis. Reasonable reviewers could classify this as 'partial success' given the substantially attenuated effect size and heavy confounding, but 'success' is defensible since the directional finding holds and the authors themselves treat it as supportive of the original.

description: Treatment of agoraphobics by exposure in cohesive groups produces continuing improvement during the follow-up period, resulting in unusually large overall clinical improvement

original_title: Group exposure (flooding) in vivo for agoraphobia
replication_authors: Teasdale JD; Walsh PA; Lancashire M.; Mathews AM
replication_title: Group Exposure for Agoraphobics: A Replication Study
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'The present study failed to replicate the unusually large overall improvement, and the continuing improvement during follow-up, reported by Hand et al (1974), for treatment by exposure in cohesive groups.' The replication followed the same design and procedure as the original, with only minor exceptions (no unstructured condition; complete follow-up data available from all groups).

description: Psychiatric patients assessed with the Delusions-Symptoms-States Inventory (DSSI) fit Foulds and Bedford's hierarchy model, and that delusions of Contrition (dC) and state of Depression (sD) have an inclusive, non-reflexive relationship (nearly all dCs have sD, but not all sDs have dC)

original_title: The classification of depressive illness: a re-evaluation
replication_authors: V. E. Bagshaw; V. E. Bagshaw
replication_title: A Replication Study of Foulds' and Bedford's Hierarchical Model of Depression
explanation: The paper is explicitly titled 'A Replication Study of Foulds' and Bedford's Hierarchical Model of Depression' and states 'The aim of this study is to replicate that of Foulds and Bedford.' The Discussion section confirms: 'Confirming Foulds and Bedford, all the results show that the relationship between dC and sD is an inclusive, non-reflexive one,' with 92.3% of 78 patients fitting the hierarchy (vs. 93.3% in the original).

description: Non-psychotic psychiatric out-patients have significant deficiencies in personal social networks (fewer attachment figures, close relatives, good friends) and spend less time in social interaction compared to general population controls

replication_title: Social Networks, Attachments and Support in Minor Affective Disorders: A Replication
explanation: The paper is explicitly titled 'A Replication' and uses the same design and instruments as the original Canberra study but in a Dublin population. The Discussion concludes: 'the overall pattern of results was remarkably similar in both studies, so that in general, it can be said that the present findings confirm those of the earlier study.' The first hypothesis (deficiencies in social networks) was confirmed, though the second hypothesis (deficiency greater for principal attachment figure) was not.

explanation: The authors explicitly state 'the prevalence rates found for bulimic episodes, self-induced vomiting and bulimia nervosa were very similar to those found in the earlier study,' with the replication finding 27.1%, 2.4%, and 1.8% respectively — all non-significant differences confirmed by chi-square statistics.

description: Sibling pairs with paternally derived schizophrenia are significantly more likely to be of the same sex than maternally derived pairs, supporting a pseudoautosomal locus for schizophrenia
original_authors: Crow, T.J.; et al.
original_title: Pseudoautosomal locus for psychosis: evidence from sibling pairs with paternally derived schizophrenia
replication_authors: Gorwood P.; Leboyer M.; d'Amato T.; Jay M.; Campion D.; Hillaire D.; Mallet J.; Feingold J.
replication_title: Evidence for a Pseudoautosomal Locus for Schizophrenia
explanation: The paper explicitly states 'In order to replicate the study by Crow et al (1989)' and found a significant excess of same-sex pairs in paternally derived sibships (χ²=5.76, P<0.02 with weighted-pair correction). The authors conclude: 'Although our results achieved only slight statistical significance, they confirm the possible involvement of the pseudoautosomal region in the aetiology of schizophrenia.'

replication_title: Expressed Emotion and Schizophrenia in Italy
explanation: The authors explicitly aimed 'to replicate the EE findings in an Italian setting' and, after adjusting the EOI cut-off to culturally appropriate values, found that high-EE families had significantly higher readmission rates (χ²=4.10, P<0.05), concluding that their findings 'appear to concur with the results of most expressed emotion studies.'

replication_authors: Donno R.; Parker G.; Gilmour J.; Skuse DH

Social communication deficits in disruptive primary-school
                        children
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'The main aim of our replication study was to confirm the provisional conclusions of the original study' and conclude 'This study replicates previous findings indicating that a relatively high proportion of children with severe and persistent disruptive behaviour have social communication impairments.' Significantly more disruptive than comparison children obtained scores in the clinical range on the CCC pragmatic composite (p = 0.001, parent data), and 35% of disruptive children met criteria for an autism-spectrum disorder.

explanation: None of the five SNPs showed a statistically significant association in either the Japanese or Singaporean replication cohorts (p-values ranged from 0.34 to 1.00, uncorrected), which the authors themselves attribute to 'replication failure' due to small sample size. However, directional consistency was observed for 3/5 SNPs in the Japanese cohort and 4/5 in the Singaporean cohort, and a combined analysis yielded stronger associations for two SNPs (rs8032978 and rs7406710, P combined = 4.92×10⁻⁵ and 5.50×10⁻⁵), leading the authors to conclude these 'could be predictive markers' rather than definitively claiming replication failure.

explanation: The replication found no significant relationship between exaggerated press release advice and exaggerated news advice (difference = 11%, 95% CI = -9.9% to 31.9%; OR = 0.7, 95% CI 0.3–1.5). explanation: The replication found a strong association: when press releases contained exaggerated causal language, 82% of associated news articles also contained exaggeration vs. 16% when not exaggerated (OR = 23.7, 95% CI 9.0–62.2). The authors state: 'The results for causal claims were highly similar to those in [23].'

explanation: Reviewer verified: The paper explicitly states it 'successfully replicated the positive results for 2-SNP or 3-SNP haplotypes that included rs12421026 (S7)' from the original family-based study [14]. Haplotype associations were replicated with very high significance in both the initial cohort (P=3.54e-10 for S4-S7) and the independent replication cohort (P=4.06e-11 for S4-S7), with consistent direction of effects. However, the single-marker associations for rs3026390 and rs3026393 reported in [14] did NOT replicate. The authors explain this is expected because the individual SNPs are likely not causal variants—the haplotypes tag the causal variants via LD. Classified as 'success' rather than 'inconclusive' because: (1) the core biological finding (PAX6 haplotype association with high myopia) replicated strongly across two independent cohorts; (2) the authors explicitly frame this as a successful replication; (3) haplotype analysis is the more powerful and informative test in this low-LD region. Replication type is 'close extension' because the study design changed from family-based to case-control, and the study examined a broader set of SNPs and regulatory regions.

explanation: Reviewer assessment: Changed result from 'inconclusive' to 'successful' and upgraded confidence to 'high'. The paper's title explicitly claims successful replication ('Polymorphisms in RYBP and AOAH Genes Are Associated with Chronic Rhinosinusitis in a Chinese Population: A Replication Study'), and the conclusion states 'We replicate several genes which were proved to be associated with CRS in Caucasian population in a Chinese population, suggesting a common basis.' The two primary candidate genes — RYBP (rs4532099, P=2.15E-06, OR=2.59) and AOAH (rs4504543, P=0.0001152, OR=0.58) — survived stringent Bonferroni correction for 49 simultaneous tests. IRAK4 SNPs showed nominal significance (P~0.02) but did not survive multiple testing correction; IL1RL1 was only nominally significant in one subgroup. While not all tested genes replicated, partial replication of the strongest original signals is the expected pattern for cross-ethnic GWAS replication. The authors unambiguously frame this as a successful replication. explanation: Reviewer verified: The paper explicitly self-identifies as a replication study (title: 'Validation of Type 2 Diabetes Risk Variants...A Replication Study and Meta-Analysis'). Authors genotyped 24 European GWAS-identified T2DM risk variants in 3,040 Han Chinese (1,502 cases, 1,518 controls) and confirmed 10 of 24 variants via meta-analysis pooling 20 Han Chinese studies (N up to ~40,000 per variant). Authors conclude: 'we confirmed the association of 10 genetic risk variants identified from European GWAS in Han Chinese' with similar effect sizes but different allele frequencies. Result classified as 'success' because the authors frame the finding positively and confirming 10/24 variants with similar ORs across ethnic populations is standard for cross-population GWAS replication (the 14 unconfirmed variants had very low statistical power due to rare allele frequencies in Han Chinese). Confidence kept at medium because: (1) the 'original' is actually multiple European GWAS (refs 3-8), not just Zeggini et al. 2008, making this a simplification; (2) partial replication (10/24) could also be framed as 'mixed' though the authors' own interpretation is clearly success. Subdiscipline corrected from 'pharmacology and toxicology' to 'genetics' — this is a genetic epidemiology study with no pharmacological component.

description: Carriers of the S/Lg allele of the 5-HTTLPR polymorphism who experienced childhood trauma show biased information processing (cognitive/emotional) as an intermediate phenotype for depression, demonstrating a gene-environment interaction effect
original_authors: Vrijsen JN; van Oostrom I.; Arias-Vásquez A.; Franke B.; Becker ES; Speckens A.

replication_title: Automatic approach-avoidance tendencies as a candidate intermediate phenotype for depression: Associations with childhood trauma and the 5-HTTLPR transporter polymorphism
explanation: Reviewer verified: The authors explicitly call this a 'conceptual replication' (abstract and Introduction). The original study (Vrijsen et al. 2014, ref [20]) examined 5-HTTLPR × childhood trauma on cognitive processing biases (attention, memory, interpretation); this paper extends to approach-avoidance tendencies — a different DV but same G×E framework, appropriately classified as conceptual replication. Result classification 'inconclusive' is correct: while the three-way interaction (Genotype × Trauma × Facial expression) reached significance (p = .034, η² = .042) and survived robustness checks, the pattern only 'partly supports' the original findings — avoidance was found for sad but not angry faces (contrary to expectations from Seidel et al.), no main effect of childhood trauma was found, and an 'unexpected' pattern emerged where LaLa without trauma avoided sad faces more than LaLa with trauma. The authors themselves use 'tentative,' 'preliminary,' and 'explorative' repeatedly and conclude 'replications using larger samples are needed.' Confidence remains 'medium' because the ambiguity is genuine — reasonable reviewers could classify this as either partial success or inconclusive given the mixed pattern of results.

Moreno-Ramos; Sara Manrique-Arija; María del Carmen Ordoñez; Juan Jose Alegre-Sancho; Javier Narvaez; Federico Navarro-Sarabia; Virginia Moreira; Lara Valor; Rosa Garcia-Portales; Ana Marquez; Juan J. Gomez-Reino; Javier Martin; Antonio Gonzalez
replication_title: Evaluation of 12 GWAS-drawn SNPs as biomarkers of rheumatoid arthritis response to TNF inhibitors. A potential SNP association with response to etanercept
explanation: The CD84 rs6427528 SNP was not significantly associated with etanercept response in the replication cohort (B = -0.04, 95% CI (-0.43, 0.76), p = 0.6). The Discussion notes this SNP 'showed the strongest standing as biomarker before our study' but 'the meta-analysis of all results has shown a very weakened association,' and the replication itself failed to find significance.

description: Loot box spending is positively linked to problem gambling severity in gamers, such that the more individuals spend on loot boxes, the more severe their problem gambling
original_authors: Zendle, David; Cairns, Paul
original_title: Video game loot boxes are linked to problem gambling: Results of a large-scale survey
replication_authors: David Zendle; Paul Cairns
replication_title: Loot boxes are again linked to problem gambling: Results of a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'This research replicates that relationship and suggests that it remains in existence even when a sample is unaware of the fact that research concerns loot boxes and gambling.' The replication found η² = 0.051 compared to the original η² = 0.054, a nearly identical effect size, confirming the direction and magnitude of the original finding.

description: Male participants solve virtual mazes significantly faster and with fewer errors than female participants, with gender differences in error rates increasing across trials as men and women learn differently
original_authors: Scott D. Moffat; Elizabeth Hampson; Maria Hatzipantelis
original_title: Navigation in a "virtual" maze: Sex differences and correlation with psychometric measures of spatial ability in humans
replication_authors: Bernd Huber; Krzysztof Z. Gajos
replication_title: Conducting online virtual environment experiments with uncompensated, unsupervised samples
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'We replicated results from the original study for both completion time between gender, as well as error rates,' with significant gender effects on completion time (F(1,518)=63.2, p<.0001) and error rates (F(1,518)=35.2, p<.0001). The study qualifies as conceptual because it moved from a supervised lab setting to an unsupervised online platform with uncompensated participants and adapted controls.

description: Participants assigned taller avatars in a virtual environment behave more confidently in a negotiation task (ultimatum game), offering more skewed splits in their favor and more readily rejecting unfair offers
original_authors: Nick Yee; Jeremy N. Bailenson; Nicolas Ducheneaut
original_title: The Proteus effect: Implications of transformed digital self-representation on online and offline behavior
replication_authors: Bernd Huber; Krzysztof Z. Gajos
replication_title: Conducting online virtual environment experiments with uncompensated, unsupervised samples
explanation: The authors state they 'were able to replicate the results in the original paper at least partially, with some decrease in effect size.' Split 2 results aligned with the original (significant effect of height), but the Unfair Offer analysis did not replicate (p>0.17 vs. significant in original), and effect sizes were substantially smaller (d=0.34 vs. d=1.23 in original).

description: PEPFAR funding (HIV development assistance) is associated with a significant decrease in all-cause adult mortality in PEPFAR focus countries compared to non-focus countries in Sub-Saharan Africa (1998-2008)
original_authors: Eran Bendavid; Charles B. Holmes; Jay Bhattacharya; Grant Miller
original_title: HIV development assistance and adult mortality in Africa
replication_authors: Nicholas A. Hein; Danstan S. Bagenda; Jiangtao Luo
replication_title: The President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief and adult mortality: A replication study of HIV development assistance effects in Sub-Saharan African countries
explanation: The authors performed a pure replication using the original authors' data and methods, closely reproducing the main finding (OR=0.84 for PEPFAR vs. non-PEPFAR mortality). The conclusion explicitly states: 'Our replication study supports the findings of BHBM' and 'we cautiously agree with the BHBM findings that PEPFAR is associated with a reduction in all-cause adult mortality.'

description: PEPFAR funding (HIV development assistance) is associated with a significant decrease in all-cause adult mortality in PEPFAR focus countries compared to non-focus countries in Sub-Saharan Africa (1998-2008)
original_authors: Eran Bendavid; Charles B. Holmes; Jay Bhattacharya; Grant Miller
original_title: HIV development assistance and adult mortality in Africa
replication_authors: Nicholas A. Hein; Danstan S. Bagenda; Jiangtao Luo
replication_title: The President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief and adult mortality: A replication study of HIV development assistance effects in Sub-Saharan African countries
explanation: Reviewer verified: The MEA applied BHBM's methods to the Duber study period (2000-2006). The fully adjusted model found OR=0.87, CI 0.75-1.01, p=0.07 — 'just outside the bounds of significance' per the authors. The unadjusted and country-adjusted models were significant (OR=0.86, p=0.04), but the most rigorous model (country + individual covariates) was not. Authors attribute non-significance to smaller sample size over a shorter period and note the point estimate falls within the original CI. 'Inconclusive' is the correct classification: the effect direction is consistent and less-adjusted models are significant, but the key fully-adjusted model crosses the null. This ambiguity is genuine and inherent to the analysis.

description: Leaf-derived callus of Cannabis sativa (high-THC genotype MX) can regenerate shoots at a 96.6% response rate with an average of 12.3 shoots per explant using a two-step protocol with MS medium containing NAA and TDZ for callus induction followed by MS with TDZ for shoot induction
original_authors: Hemant Lata; Suman Chandra; Ikhlas Khan; Mahmoud ElSohly
original_title: High frequency plant regeneration from leaf derived callus of high Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol yielding Cannabis sativa L
replication_authors: Adrian S. Monthony; Sean T. Kyne; Christopher M. Grainger; Andrew Maxwell P. Jones
replication_title: Recalcitrance of Cannabis sativa to de novo regeneration; a multi-genotype replication study
explanation: The replication authors explicitly state: 'we were unable to successfully initiate regeneration by transferring callus to MS medium supplemented with 0.5 μM TDZ in any of the 10 tested genotypes.' While callus induction was successful (100% across all genotypes, comparable to the original), the critical shoot organogenesis step failed entirely — 0% regeneration versus the original's claimed 96.6%.

description: Fluid arm movements (tracing curved line-drawings) enhance creative fluency (number of alternative uses generated) compared to non-fluid arm movements (tracing angular line-drawings)
original_authors: Michael L. Slepian; Nalini Ambady
original_title: Fluid movement and creativity
replication_authors: Shu Imaizumi; Ubuka Tagami; Yi Yang
replication_title: Fluid movements enhance creative fluency: A replication of Slepian and Ambady (2012)
explanation: The authors confirmed the fluency finding: 'participants who traced curved line-drawings subsequently generated a larger number of alternative uses of printed newspapers than did those who traced angular line-drawings' (t(58) = 2.34, p = 0.023, d = 0.60). The authors state 'our results replicated and further demonstrated the facilitative effect of fluid arm movements on fluency.'

description: Fluid arm movements (tracing curved line-drawings) enhance creative originality (rated originality of alternative uses generated) compared to non-fluid arm movements (tracing angular line-drawings)
original_authors: Michael L. Slepian; Nalini Ambady
original_title: Fluid movement and creativity
replication_authors: Shu Imaizumi; Ubuka Tagami; Yi Yang
replication_title: Fluid movements enhance creative fluency: A replication of Slepian and Ambady (2012)
explanation: The replication found no significant effect of fluid arm movements on originality (t(58) = 1.16, p = 0.250, d = 0.30). The authors conclude 'we did not find any effects on originality' and 'we partially replicated Experiment 1 of Slepian and Ambady,' contrasting with the original's d = 0.87.

description: Women with MAOA-L (low activity) variants are less likely to behave as free-riders than MAOA-H carriers in a public goods game using the strategy method
original_authors: Vanessa Mertins; Andrea B. Schote; Jobst Meyer
original_title: Variants of the monoamine oxidase A gene (MAOA) predict free-riding behavior in women in a strategic public goods experiment
original_journal: Journal of Neuroscience, Psychology, and Economics
replication_authors: María I. Rivera-Hechem; Carlos Rodríguez-Sickert; Ricardo A. Guzmán; Tadeo Ramírez-Parada; Felipe Benavides; Víctor Landaeta-Torres; Mauricio Aspé-Sánchez; Gabriela M. Repetto
replication_title: No association between genetic variants in MAOA, OXTR, and AVPR1a and cooperative strategies
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Discussion: 'our findings did not replicate previous results by Mertins et al. [27] for MAOA-uVNTR.' No significant association between MAOA-uVNTR and cooperative strategies was found (p ≥ 0.145, Fisher exact test) in the admixed Latino sample (n=188).

description: Showing participants images comparing the current (degraded) environment to the past (pristine) environment—rather than comparing the current (pristine) environment to the future (degraded) environment—increases pro-environmental attitudes among political conservatives
original_authors: Matthew Baldwin; Joris Lammers
original_title: Past-focused environmental comparisons promote proenvironmental outcomes for conservatives
replication_authors: Samantha K. Stanley; Anna Klas; Edward J. R. Clarke; Iain Walker
replication_title: The effects of a temporal framing manipulation on environmentalism: A replication and extension
explanation: In Study One (N=535, US), the authors found only one significant temporal framing × political orientation interaction (on climate change certainty), not on pro-environmental attitudes. The authors conclude: 'we found limited evidence that past comparisons (relative to future comparisons) increase proenvironmentalism among those with a more conservative political ideology.' They explicitly state failing to replicate the main effect.

description: Showing participants images comparing the current (degraded) environment to the past (pristine) environment—rather than comparing the current (pristine) environment to the future (degraded) environment—increases pro-environmental attitudes among political conservatives
original_authors: Matthew Baldwin; Joris Lammers
original_title: Past-focused environmental comparisons promote proenvironmental outcomes for conservatives
replication_authors: Samantha K. Stanley; Anna Klas; Edward J. R. Clarke; Iain Walker
replication_title: The effects of a temporal framing manipulation on environmentalism: A replication and extension
explanation: In Study Two (N=1102, UK), a pre-registered large-scale replication, the authors found no significant temporal framing × political orientation interactions for pro-environmental outcomes. They conclude: 'Our results still do not support the image-based temporal framing manipulation as an effective frame to induce pro-environmentalism among conservatives.' An unexpected backfire effect was found for liberals.

description: People with higher problem gambling severity spend more money on video game loot boxes in real-world/physical stores than those with lower problem gambling severity
original_authors: David Zendle; Paul Cairns
original_title: Video game loot boxes are linked to problem gambling: Results of a large-scale survey
replication_authors: David Zendle; Lukasz Walasek; Paul Cairns; Rachel Meyer; Aaron Drummond
replication_title: Links between problem gambling and spending on booster packs in collectible card games: A conceptual replication of research on loot boxes
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'spending money on booster packs does not appear to be linked to problem gambling in the same way that spending money on loot boxes is.' The equivalence test rejected the hypothesis that the effect was of practical importance (η² = 0.004, p = 0.110 for physical store spending), failing to replicate the loot box–problem gambling link in the CCG booster pack context.

description: People with higher problem gambling severity spend more money on video game loot boxes in digital/online stores than those with lower problem gambling severity
original_authors: David Zendle; Paul Cairns
original_title: Video game loot boxes are linked to problem gambling: Results of a large-scale survey
replication_authors: David Zendle; Lukasz Walasek; Paul Cairns; Rachel Meyer; Aaron Drummond
replication_title: Links between problem gambling and spending on booster packs in collectible card games: A conceptual replication of research on loot boxes
explanation: Although a statistically significant effect was found (p = 0.035), it was trivial in magnitude (η² = 0.008), well below the η² = 0.04 threshold for clinical relevance, and equivalence tests confirmed the effect was not practically important. The authors conclude this represents 'a trivial in magnitude relationship' that does not replicate the meaningful loot box–problem gambling link.

description: Children born late preterm show differential susceptibility to the Living Letters digital literacy intervention, falling behind peers in a control condition but outperforming them when assigned to the intervention (interaction effect between late preterm birth and condition)
original_authors: Inge Merkelbach; Rachel D. Plak; Ralph C.A. Rippe
original_title: Reproducibility of young learners' susceptibility to the learning context
replication_authors: Ralph C. A. Rippe; Inge Merkelbach
replication_title: Planned missing data in early literacy interventions: A replication study with an additional gold standard
explanation: The authors explicitly state 'Results were replicated, however not in all planned missing data models fitted to the data.' The key interaction was significant only in one of three models (writing-only gold standard, p = .019), marginally non-significant in another (p = .053), and non-significant in the baseline model (p = .154), indicating partial support only under specific analytical conditions.

description: The generically-intended masculine possessive pronoun zijn ('his') does not trigger a gender inference or cause a male bias when used with the indefinite pronoun iedereen ('everyone') in Dutch eye-tracking reading tasks
original_authors: Theresa Redl; Anita Eerland; Ted J. M. Sanders
original_title: The processing of the Dutch masculine generic zijn 'his' across stereotype contexts: An eye-tracking study
replication_authors: Theresa Redl; Stefan L. Frank; Peter de Swart; Helen de Hoop
replication_title: The male bias of a generically-intended masculine pronoun: Evidence from eye-tracking and sentence evaluation
explanation: The current study found a partial male bias (for male participants in stereotypically neutral contexts only), contrary to the original's null result, but not the full male bias across conditions hypothesized. The authors state: 'we did find evidence for a male bias early in processing, but for male participants and in stereotypically neutral contexts only,' describing the overall picture as suggesting zijn 'his' 'can cause a male bias under certain conditions.'

description: The mere presence of a mobile phone (vs. a notebook) impairs relationship quality (sense of connection, trust, and perceived empathy) between strangers during a conversation
original_authors: Andrew K. Przybylski; Netta Weinstein
original_title: Can you connect with me now? How the presence of mobile communication technology influences face-to-face conversation quality
original_journal: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
replication_authors: Claire Linares; Anne-Laure Sellier
replication_title: How bad is the mere presence of a phone? A replication of Przybylski and Weinstein (2013) and an extension to creativity
explanation: Across two studies (N=356 participants, 136 groups), the authors found no significant effect of the mere presence of a smartphone on any relationship quality measure. The conclusion states: 'We did not replicate Przybylski and Weinstein's [12] finding that the mere presence of a mobile device impairs relationship quality.'

description: Machine learning algorithms (random forests, gradient boosted decision trees, XGBoost, logistic regression) with feature selection methods can predict treatment-resistant depression (TRD) in MDD patients from clinical data in the STAR*D dataset with balanced accuracy of 64–71%
original_authors: Zhi Nie; Srinivasan Vairavan; Vaibhav A. Narayan; Jieping Ye; Qingqin S. Li
original_title: Predictive modeling of treatment resistant depression using data from STAR*D and an independent clinical study
replication_authors: John-Jose Nunez; Teyden T. Nguyen; Yihan Zhou; Bo Cao; Raymond T. Ng; Jun Chen; Benicio N. Frey; Roumen Milev; Daniel J. Müller; Susan Rotzinger; Claudio N. Soares; Rudolf Uher; Sidney H. Kennedy; Raymond W. Lam
replication_title: Replication of machine learning methods to predict treatment outcome with antidepressant medications in patients with major depressive disorder from STAR*D and CAN-BIND-1
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'We successfully replicate the prior Nie et al cross-validation results using a newer version of their data that is publicly available.' Their replicated models achieved balanced accuracies of 70–73% and AUCs of 0.76–0.81, numerically similar to or slightly higher than Nie et al.'s 64–71% and 0.73–0.78, which the authors interpret as a successful replication despite small differences due to using a newer dataset version and different train/test split method.

description: Chinese-English bilingual preschool children outperform English monolingual children in rule-switching on the Dimensional Change Card Sort (DCCS) task, demonstrating a bilingual advantage in cognitive flexibility/executive function
original_authors: Ellen Bialystok; Michelle M. Martin
original_title: Attention and inhibition in bilingual children: Evidence from the dimensional change card sort task
replication_authors: Anahita Shokrkon; Elena Nicoladis
replication_title: Absence of a bilingual cognitive flexibility advantage: A replication study in preschoolers
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the Conclusion: 'The present study did not replicate the bilingual advantage on executive function performance found in [Bialystok & Martin, 2004].' The language group main effect was non-significant (F(1,39) = 2.40, p = .12) with no bilingual advantage found on any of the four DCCS conditions.

description: Real-time sentence processing is sensitive to strong island constraints, such that readers do not form active filler-gap dependencies inside strong islands (e.g., relative clause islands), as evidenced by the absence of a filled-gap processing cost within island domains
original_authors: Laurie A. Stowe
original_title: Parsing WH-constructions: evidence for on-line gap location
replication_authors: Derya Cokal; Patrick Sturt
replication_title: The real-time status of strong and weak islands
explanation: The authors explicitly describe Experiment 1 as providing 'a conceptual replication of previous studies showing that real time processing is sensitive to strong islands,' and conclude: 'we have replicated previous findings that on-line sentence comprehension is sensitive to strong islands (Experiment 1).' The significant interaction between islandhood and dependency type in the spill-over region confirmed the predicted pattern.

description: Inquiring about test takers' gender after rather than before a standardized mathematics test reduces stereotype threat and improves women's test performance
original_authors: Lawrence J. Stricker; William C. Ward
original_title: Stereotype threat, inquiring about test takers' ethnicity and gender, and standardized test performance
replication_authors: Matthew Inglis; Steven O’Hagan
replication_title: Stereotype threat, gender and mathematics attainment: A conceptual replication of Stricker & Ward
explanation: The authors explicitly state they conducted a 'conceptual replication of Stricker and Ward's study' and 'found no evidence for this effect'. The preregistered ANOVA found no significant version-by-gender interaction (F(1,1165)=0.525, p=.469, η²=.000), and a Bayesian analysis provided strong evidence for the null (BF₀₁s = 8.123 and 46.052).

description: Resting state functional MRI brain connectivity measures differ significantly between children who report anhedonia and controls, with 11 specific rsfMRI connectivity measures identified as significantly associated with childhood anhedonia in the ABCD 1.0 study sample
original_authors: Narun Pornpattananangkul; Ellen Leibenluft; Daniel S. Pine; Argyris Stringaris
original_title: Association between childhood anhedonia and alterations in large-scale resting-state networks and task-evoked activation
replication_authors: Yi Zhou; Narun Pat; Michael C. Neale
replication_title: Associations between resting state functional brain connectivity and childhood anhedonia: A reproduction and replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in their abstract that 'effect sizes for most rsfMRI measures were drastically reduced in replication analyses' and the abstract concludes 'The most statistically significant associations between anhedonia and rsfMRI connectivity measures found in the ABCD 1.0 sample tended to be non-replicable and inflated.' In the Discussion, they confirm: 'we were mostly unable to replicate them using a larger independent subset of the full ABCD 4.0 release sample.'

description: Stimuli of greater light intensity magnitude cause children to perceive their duration as longer in a simultaneous duration assessment task (magnitude effect)
original_authors: Iris Levin
original_title: Interference of time-related and unrelated cues with duration comparisons of young children: analysis of Piaget's formulation of the relation of time and speed
replication_authors: Amihai Gottlieb; Dan Zakay
replication_title: The effect of magnitude in a simultaneous duration assessment task among children – a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state in the conclusion: 'the present studies successfully replicate the results reported by Levin [4] and Levin and Gilat [5] on the existence of magnitude effects in simultaneous duration tasks.' The Study 1 chi-square analysis revealed a significant magnitude effect pattern (χ²(2) = 15.8, p < .001), consistent with the original finding. The replication used a different population (Arabic-speaking children aged 7-12 vs. Hebrew-speaking children aged 4-7) and adapted stimuli, making it a close extension.

description: The additive effect of multiple magnitude cues (light intensity and size) on children's duration comparisons in a simultaneous assessment task produces a magnitude effect
original_authors: Iris Levin; Izhak Gilat
original_title: A developmental analysis of early time concepts: the equivalence and additivity of the effect of interfering cues on duration comparisons of young children
replication_authors: Amihai Gottlieb; Dan Zakay
replication_title: The effect of magnitude in a simultaneous duration assessment task among children – a replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude that 'the present studies successfully replicate the results reported by Levin [4] and Levin and Gilat [5] on the existence of magnitude effects in simultaneous duration tasks.' The Study 1 results showed a significant overall magnitude effect pattern (χ²(2) = 15.8, p < .001), replicating the core findings of both Levin papers. The replication was conducted with Arabic-speaking children aged 7-12 in a different cultural context, qualifying it as a close extension.

description: Children reproduce the duration of high-intensity lightbulbs as longer than low-intensity lightbulbs of equal duration (magnitude effect in duration reproduction task)
original_authors: Dan Zakay
original_title: The role of attention in children's time perception
replication_authors: Amihai Gottlieb; Dan Zakay
replication_title: The effect of magnitude in a simultaneous duration assessment task among children – a replication study
explanation: Despite acknowledging 'experiment two was not an exact replication of experiment 2 of the Zakay [12] study', the authors report that 'the results of both experiments are similar, as both showed a magnitude effect.' Study 2 found a significant main effect of intensity (F(1,42) = 70.2, p < .001, ηp² = .62), confirming that children reproduced high-intensity bulb durations as longer. The replication used different stimuli intensities and much longer durations (20/30s vs. 3/6s) with a different cultural/linguistic population.

description: Need for Cognition (NFC) and Action Orientation (AO) are correlated predictors of Self-Control in university students, with AO partially mediating the relation between NFC and Self-Control
original_authors: Julia Grass; Florian Krieger; Philipp Paulus; Samuel Greiff; Anja Strobel; Alexander Strobel
original_title: Thinking in action: Need for Cognition predicts Self-Control together with Action Orientation
replication_authors: Jonne Colling; Rachel Wollschläger; Ulrich Keller; Julia Grass; Anja Strobel; Franzis Preckel; Antoine Fischbach
replication_title: The relation between Self-Control, Need for Cognition and Action Orientation in secondary school students: A conceptual replication study
explanation: The authors explicitly state they 'replicated the findings that Need for Cognition and Action Orientation predict Self-Control and that Action Orientation partially mediates the relation between Need for Cognition and Self-Control' in a younger population (9th graders) using age-appropriate measures. The partial mediation model was confirmed, and the moderation finding (unexpected from the original) is an extension rather than a contradiction of the core replication target.

description: Cues of perceived trustworthiness in European portraits increased over time during the early modern and modern periods, and this increase is correlated with economic development (GDP per capita)
original_authors: Lou Safra; Coralie Chevallier; Julie Grèzes; Nicolas Baumard
original_title: Tracking historical changes in trustworthiness using machine learning analyses of facial cues in paintings
replication_authors: Léonard Guillou; Lou Safra; Nicolas Baumard
replication_title: Using portraits to quantify the changes of generalized social trust in European history: A replication study
explanation: Study 1 (N=966 European sovereign portraits) successfully replicated the increase in modeled perceived facial trustworthiness over time (b = 0.182, t(201) = 4.40, p < .001). The authors explicitly conclude: 'Study 1 did replicate the results on the association between time and modeled perceived facial trustworthiness, using a database controlled for the social status of the sitters.' The GDP effect was not significant when controlling for time, a partial divergence from the original.

description: Cues of perceived trustworthiness in European portraits increased over time during the early modern and modern periods, and this increase is correlated with economic development (GDP per capita)
original_authors: Lou Safra; Coralie Chevallier; Julie Grèzes; Nicolas Baumard
original_title: Tracking historical changes in trustworthiness using machine learning analyses of facial cues in paintings
replication_authors: Léonard Guillou; Lou Safra; Nicolas Baumard
replication_title: Using portraits to quantify the changes of generalized social trust in European history: A replication study
explanation: Study 2 (N=2,291 Château de Versailles portraits) failed to replicate the main finding. The authors explicitly state: 'This study fails to replicate the results from Safra et al.' No significant effect of time was found (b = -0.02, t(759) = -0.85, p > .250), and no significant effect of GDP was found either with or without controlling for time.

description: Darkness (compared to light) increases dishonest behavior, attributed to participants' heightened perceived anonymity in dimmer environments
original_authors: Chen-Bo Zhong; Vanessa K. Bohns; Francesca Gino
original_title: Good lamps are the best police: Darkness increases dishonesty and self-interested behavior
replication_authors: Huanxu Liu; Yuning Zhou; Yuki Yamada
replication_title: Darkness promotes dishonesty in a coin toss task: A pre-registered conceptual replication of Experiment 1 of Zhong, Bohns, and Gino (2010)
explanation: The authors explicitly state: 'We successfully replicated the original experiment that darkness was found to promote dishonest behavior, albeit with more precise control over the lighting conditions, and by using another task.' The replication used a coin toss task (different from the original Matrix Task) and found a significant effect of darkness on dishonesty (t(100) = 1.885, p = .031, Cohen's d = 0.373). The paper's title itself labels this a 'pre-registered conceptual replication.'

description: PD patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) exhibit increased cortical thinning over time compared to PD patients without MCI (mainly right temporal regions, insula, and inferior frontal gyrus) and compared to healthy controls (mainly right temporal regions and supplementary motor area)
original_authors: Alexandru Hanganu; Christophe Bedetti; Clotilde Degroot; Béatriz Mejia-Constain; Anne-Louise Lafontaine; Valérie Soland; Sylvain Chouinard; Marie-Andrée Bruneau; Samira Mellah; Sylvie Belleville; Oury Monchi
original_title: Mild cognitive impairment is linked with faster rate of cortical thinning in patients with Parkinson's disease longitudinally
replication_authors: Andrzej Sokołowski; Nikhil Bhagwat; Yohan Chatelain; Mathieu Dugré; Alexandru Hanganu; Oury Monchi; Brent McPherson; Michelle Wang; Jean-Baptiste Poline; Madeleine Sharp; Tristan Glatard
replication_title: Longitudinal brain structure changes in Parkinson’s disease: A replication study
explanation: The authors replicated the PD-MCI vs PD-non-MCI cortical thinning differences (right MTG and insula overlap with original), but did not replicate the group differences involving healthy controls: 'we have replicated the differences in the rate of cortical thinning between the PD-MCI and PD-non-MCI groups (Finding 1)...However, we did not replicate the group differences involving the HC group.'

description: The rate of cortical thinning correlates with change in MoCA cognitive scores in PD patients, particularly in bilateral temporal lobe, right occipital medial lobe, and left postcentral gyrus
original_authors: Alexandru Hanganu; Christophe Bedetti; Clotilde Degroot; Béatriz Mejia-Constain; Anne-Louise Lafontaine; Valérie Soland; Sylvain Chouinard; Marie-Andrée Bruneau; Samira Mellah; Sylvie Belleville; Oury Monchi
original_title: Mild cognitive impairment is linked with faster rate of cortical thinning in patients with Parkinson's disease longitudinally
replication_authors: Andrzej Sokołowski; Nikhil Bhagwat; Yohan Chatelain; Mathieu Dugré; Alexandru Hanganu; Oury Monchi; Brent McPherson; Michelle Wang; Jean-Baptiste Poline; Madeleine Sharp; Tristan Glatard
replication_title: Longitudinal brain structure changes in Parkinson’s disease: A replication study
explanation: A positive correlation was found between MoCA scores and cortical thinning of the left inferior temporal and precentral gyri (the ITG cluster partially overlapping with the original study), but not in the exact same regions. The authors conclude 'we have replicated the original vertex-wise results (Findings 1 and 2 in [15]) to a certain extent.'

description: PD patients with MCI show increased loss of amygdala and nucleus accumbens volumes as well as overall cortical thickness compared to healthy controls
original_authors: Alexandru Hanganu; Christophe Bedetti; Clotilde Degroot; Béatriz Mejia-Constain; Anne-Louise Lafontaine; Valérie Soland; Sylvain Chouinard; Marie-Andrée Bruneau; Samira Mellah; Sylvie Belleville; Oury Monchi
original_title: Mild cognitive impairment is linked with faster rate of cortical thinning in patients with Parkinson's disease longitudinally
replication_authors: Andrzej Sokołowski; Nikhil Bhagwat; Yohan Chatelain; Mathieu Dugré; Alexandru Hanganu; Oury Monchi; Brent McPherson; Michelle Wang; Jean-Baptiste Poline; Madeleine Sharp; Tristan Glatard
replication_title: Longitudinal brain structure changes in Parkinson’s disease: A replication study
explanation: No significant group differences were found in the change of subcortical volumes (all ps > .05). The authors explicitly state: 'Volumetric results (Findings 3 and 4 in [15]) were not replicated.'

description: Change in right amygdala and thalamus volumes correlates with change in MoCA cognitive scores in PD patients
original_authors: Alexandru Hanganu; Christophe Bedetti; Clotilde Degroot; Béatriz Mejia-Constain; Anne-Louise Lafontaine; Valérie Soland; Sylvain Chouinard; Marie-Andrée Bruneau; Samira Mellah; Sylvie Belleville; Oury Monchi
original_title: Mild cognitive impairment is linked with faster rate of cortical thinning in patients with Parkinson's disease longitudinally

description: Self-perceived loneliness is the most time-sensitive variable during COVID-19 lockdown (identified via RandomForest machine learning model) and follows a U-shaped distribution by week of lockdown in UK and Greek populations

replication_title: Self-perceived loneliness and depression during the Covid-19 pandemic: a two-wave replication study
explanation: Reviewer assessment: 'inconclusive' is appropriate and the ambiguity is genuine. The paper tests two claims from the original: (1) that loneliness is the most time-sensitive lockdown variable, and (2) that loneliness follows a U-shaped weekly pattern. For claim 1, using SVR and MLR instead of RandomForest on the same Wave 1 UK data (n=435), depression—not loneliness—was identified as most time-sensitive, contradicting the original. For claim 2, a graphical inspection of Wave 2 data (n=263) showed a qualitative U-shaped loneliness pattern, but the authors explicitly state 'no statistically meaningful insight could be derived' due to extremely small weekly cell sizes (e.g., weeks 4-8 had 0-5 participants each). The authors themselves describe these results as 'only qualitative and preliminary' and note 'graphical disparities among scores might be mere random variation.' With one finding contradicted and the other only weakly and qualitatively supported, medium confidence in an inconclusive classification is warranted.

explanation: Reviewer upgrade to high confidence. The paper is titled 'Replication Study of Candidate Genes Associated With Type 2 Diabetes Based On Genome-Wide Screening' and explicitly aims to replicate GWAS findings (refs 4-10, with Sladek et al. 2007 as the primary original) in a Japanese population. In the authors' own case-control analysis (n=908), 8 of 11 SNPs reached nominal significance; only CDKAL1 survived Bonferroni correction. However, the meta-analysis of 7 Japanese studies confirmed all 11 SNPs with Bonferroni-adjusted significance. The authors conclude unambiguously: 'Type 2 diabetes susceptibility of seven candidate genes was confirmed in Japanese. Conservation of susceptible loci for type 2 diabetes was independent of ethnic background.' Result classified as 'success' because the overall conclusion across case-control and meta-analysis is that all tested associations replicated. Classified as 'close extension' because the same genetic variants are tested in a different ethnic population (Japanese vs. European).

replication_authors: Agnieszka Maciejewska-Skrendo; Jan Mieszkowski; Andrzej Kochanowicz; Bartosz Niespodziński; Paweł Cieszczyk; Katarzyna Leźnicka; Agata Leońska-Duniec; Marek Kolbowicz; Mariusz Kaczmarczyk; Elżbieta Piskorska; Błażej Stankiewicz; Robert Stępniak; Aleksandra Mostowik; Marek Zawartka; Agata Rzeszutko-Bełzowska; Myosotis Massidda; Carla Caló; Eglė Kemerytė-Riaubienė; Marek Sawczuk
replication_title: Does the PPARA Intron 7 Gene Variant (rs4253778) Influence Performance in Power/Strength‐Oriented Athletes? A Case‐Control Replication Study in three Cohorts of European Gymnasts
explanation: Reviewer assessment: 'Inconclusive' is the correct classification and medium confidence is appropriate because the ambiguity is genuine. The paper (self-described as a 'Case-Control Replication Study') tested the same PPARA rs4253778 SNP in gymnasts from three countries. Individual cohort analyses (Polish, Italian, Lithuanian) all found NO significant differences under any inheritance model (Tables 2-4, all p > 0.05). Only when all three cohorts were pooled and only under the recessive model did the result reach significance (CC: OR = 3.33, 95% CI = 1.18-10.00, p = 0.022; Table 5). This single significant result has notable weaknesses: (1) it emerged from one of four inheritance models tested across four groupings, raising multiple-comparisons concerns; (2) the CC cell counts are tiny (9 gymnasts vs 6 controls); (3) the 95% CI is very wide and barely excludes 1.0. The authors state their results 'corroborate previous studies' but also emphasize small sample size and explicitly call for validation in larger cohorts. Reasonable readers could classify this as a weak success or a failure — the ambiguity is inherent in the data.

description: The OPTIMAL instrument (Outpatient Physical Therapy Improvement in Movement Assessment Log) demonstrates good psychometric properties — including acceptable internal consistency, known-groups validity, and convergent validity — for measuring activity limitations in patients with musculoskeletal disorders in outpatient physical therapy settings
original_authors: Andrew A. Guccione; Thelma J. Mielenz; Robert F. DeVellis; Marc S. Goldstein; Janet K. Freburger; Ricardo Pietrobon; Sarah C. Miller; Leigh F. Callahan; Kenneth Harwood; Timothy S. Carey
original_title: Development and testing of a self-report instrument to measure actions: Outpatient Physical Therapy Improvement in Movement Assessment Log (OPTIMAL)
replication_authors: Daniel L. Riddle; Paul W. Stratford; Tracy L. Carter; Joshua A. Cleland
replication_title: Psychometric Properties of the Outpatient Physical Therapy Improvement in Movement Assessment Log (OPTIMAL) in Patients With Musculoskeletal Disorders: A Replication Study With Additional Findings
explanation: The authors explicitly conclude: 'our study generally does not support use of the OPTIMAL on patients with musculoskeletal disorders' and 'the psychometric properties of the OPTIMAL are relatively unstable compared with the work of Guccione and colleagues.' While known-groups validity was partially replicated, internal consistency was substantially lower (alpha values much lower for trunk and upper-extremity subscales) and convergent validity correlations were weak (<.30 vs. .80 in the original), representing an overall failure to replicate the psychometric support for the instrument.

description: Recovering chemically dependent nurses share identifiable personal, familial, and professional characteristics including family history of dependency, academic success, sexual problems, history of depression, and recovery behaviors
original_authors: Sullivan, Eleanor
original_title: A descriptive study of nurses recovering from chemical dependency
replication_authors: Veryl Margaret Tipliski
replication_title: The Characteristics of Recovering Chemically-Dependent Manitoba Nurses
explanation: The author explicitly calls this a 'descriptive replication study' and uses an adapted version of Sullivan's survey instrument in a different national context (Manitoba, Canada vs. USA). The conclusion states: 'Numerous findings in this study do parallel the findings [from] American studies of the recovering nurse, thus adding further support to the data base,' and 'the majority of characteristics of the recovering Manitoba nurses are similar to those found in American studies, in particular, Sullivan (1987a).' Some unique characteristics were noted for the Manitoba sample.

description: Elevated urinary p-cresol concentrations are found in children with autism spectrum disorder compared to controls, reflecting abnormal gut flora fermentation of tyrosine
original_authors: Ivan K. S. Yap; Manya Angley; Kirill A. Veselkov; Elaine Holmes; John C. Lindon; Jeremy K. Nicholson
original_title: Urinary metabolic phenotyping differentiates children with autism from their unaffected siblings and age-matched controls
